signals.source_text: El Niño’s impacts can be felt globally—stunting maize harvests in Africa, prompting flooding in the United States, and causing droughts in Australia. The widespread disruption it causes makes monitoring and understanding this tropical Pacific climate phenomenon an imperative for national and economic security. Saildrone and the NOAA: National Oceanic & Atmospheric Administration ’s Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory (PMEL) recently deployed four Saildrone Explorer unmanned surface vehicles to the tropical Pacific. Working in conjunction with the Tropical Pacific Observing System, Saildrone will support NOAA’s research measuring El Niño’s strength by filling in critical data gaps that buoys, floats, and satellites do not capture. “This long-standing partnership matches the unparalleled endurance and resilience of Saildrone's unmanned surface vehicles with NOAA’s world-renowned expertise to deliver accurate, real-time observations from the equatorial Pacific—allowing scientists to better understand El Niño and forecast its global impacts,” said Matt Womble, vice president of government relations at Saildrone. By filling gaps in the existing TPOS network, Saildrone USVs give researchers a more detailed view of the complex atmospheric conditions and changes happening across the tropical Pacific. Those observations improve forecasts of El Niño’s global effects, helping governments and industries better prepare for disruptions to agriculture, shipping, infrastructure, and severe weather—all of which carry significant national and economic security consequences. Read more about the mission: https://lnkd.in/ekcHK9re
projects: Deployment of four Saildrone Explorer unmanned surface vehicles in the tropical Pacific with NOAA PMEL and the Tropical Pacific Observing System to measure El Niño and fill ocean-observation data gaps

The critical band runs 100 Hz to 5 kHz, and no single method covers it. The Engineer's Guide to Modern NVH Simulation shows how to work the full range in MSC Nastran and Actran: heavy-fluid coupling, Virtual SEA, and ODYSSEE ROMs. Preview the first pages, then download the full guide below 👇

signals.source_text: This MATLAB animation brings a 2,000-year-old idea to life. Archimedes approximated π using a circle and polygons. By doubling the number of sides, he tightened the bounds on π and got closer to its true value. While Archimedes expressed his results as fractions, this animation created in MATLAB shows the same geometric idea through decimal approximations converging toward π.
